0.x: Mother Goddess – the chief female deity
**Mother Goddess (Devi Mata):** terracotta female figurines, heavily jewelled, with fan-shaped head-dresses → **fertility cult**; probably the chief female deity.
**Sites:** Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Kot Diji, Kalibangan, Banawali (with the toy plough) and Gujarat sites; Ropar is known for the dog burial instead.

**Continuity:** the Mother Goddess cult survives in the later **Shakti cults**. "Spirit and Brahma", "ritual" and the "sacrificial system" are Vedic ideas; the Indus cult centres on the **Mother Goddess**.
Pashupati seal – the chief male deity

r: **Three-faced**, horned head-dress, seated in a **yogic posture**
**Elephant, tiger, rhinoceros, buffalo**; **two deer** below the seat; no lion
The script is undeciphered, so the reading is an inference from later Shiva worship

0.x: The **Indus people worshipped Shiva**; Indra and Varuna are Rig Vedic gods; Brahma and Vishnu are later.
**Both male and female deities** were worshipped (Mother Goddess + Pashupati).
**Idol worship began in the pre-Aryan (Harappan) period:** no temple has been found, yet idolatry was practised through figurines and seals. The Rig Vedic Aryans had **no idols or temples**.

1.x: **Pipal:** the tree most often depicted on Indus seals (a deity standing among pipal branches); the motif goes back to the **Early Harappan** phase, and the pipal is still worshipped.

**Sacred animals:** the **unicorn** (mythical one-horned animal, the commonest seal motif), the **humped bull** (next in importance), elephant, tiger, buffalo, rhinoceros; cobras and horned deities also appear. The **animals round Pashupati** were probably worshipped too.
The peacock is only a pottery motif.
**Linga and yoni:** conical stones (lingas) and **round pierced stones** (yoni) – fertility objects, possibly early Shaivite elements; found at Harappa.
**Swastika:** a seal motif, later an auspicious Hindu symbol; it has no link with the Vedic yajna.
**Seals:** mostly of **steatite**, mostly **square**; some with a hole were used as **amulets**.

r: A row of **seven fire altars** on a mud-brick platform; a **triangular terracotta cake** with a **horned deity** on one side and a **human pulling a goat by a rope** (animal sacrifice) on the other
Small pits with terracotta cakes regarded as fire altars

2.x: **⚠ Caution:** Harappan fire altars are **not conclusive proof of the later Vedic yajna**.
**Amulets:** holed seals and amulets suggest belief in **ghosts and evil forces**; deities shown in **yogic poses** → the practice of yoga and meditation.
**Burials with grave goods** point to a belief in life after death.

3.x: **Character:** a predominantly **secular** civilisation – religion present but not dominant; nature- and **fertility-oriented** worship.
**No temple** has been identified anywhere; worship was domestic or open-air (under trees).
**Undeciphered script:** every reading of Harappan religion (proto-Shiva, Mother Goddess) is inferred from later traditions.
**Continuities into Hinduism:** Shiva / Pashupati, Shakti (Mother Goddess), linga-yoni, pipal and animal veneration, yoga.
**Contrast with the Rig Veda:** Vedic religion = **male nature gods and open-air yajnas**, no idols; Harappan = Mother Goddess, idols, animal and tree worship.
**Significance:** the earliest material evidence of a Shiva-like deity, a Mother Goddess and fertility cults in India.
